Grade 7 source-sequence repair: In this lesson, first build hinged polygons using fixed strip lengths, measure and redraw a triangle and a quadrilateral, and compare overlapping copies. WorkedExamples.Question: Use sticks of lengths 4, 5, 8 cm to make a triangle and sticks 3, 4, 9 cm to try making a triangle. Explain outcomes, then draw a nonunique four-side example.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw an independent accurate geometry model, measure or construct required angles/sides/cross-sections, calculate and justify, and submit for teacher review.
Steps: Make a triangle with hinged 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm strips; measure and sketch its angles, then compare copies.

Make two quadrilaterals with consecutive sides 9, 4, 5 and 6 inches, allowing the hinge angle to change; record different diagonal lengths such as 7 and 9 inches.
Overlay the two quadrilaterals to show they are not identical, despite the same four side lengths. Explain why any 4-5-8 triangles from fixed rigid strips overlay after rotation or reflection.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A 4-5-8 triangle exists; 3-4-9 is impossible; quadrilateral side-only data can be nonunique.

WorkedExamples.Question: Two triangles each have interior angles 50°,60°,70°, but one has a 3 cm side and another the corresponding side is 6 cm. Are they identical? What additional type of measurement fixes size?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw an independent accurate geometry model, measure or construct required angles/sides/cross-sections, calculate and justify, and submit for teacher review.
Steps: Identical corresponding angles determine similarity but not absolute scale.
A 6 cm corresponding side is twice the 3 cm side, so the triangles are not congruent.

Lessons.Title: Drawing Triangles (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks Grade 7 source-aligned goal: using a straightedge, protractor or original independent digital construction, draw triangles when one angle, two angles, or two angles and one side length are specified; explain if the constraints permit zero, one (up to congruence), or more than one distinct triangle. Based on OUR/IM 2017–2019 lesson 7.7.9; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/7/9/index.html and teacher preparation https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/7/9/preparation.html. Original diagrams and tasks are independently authored, CC BY 4.0 curriculum attribution.

V13 source-specific construction repair: Draw and measure, then compare possible constructions, instead of treating this lesson primarily as side-side-side arithmetic. Given one 75° angle, or angles 75° and 45° alone, differently scaled triangles can be made. Adding a particular 5 cm corresponding side to the two angles fixes a size; simply saying 'one side 5 cm' without specifying which side can admit different sizes. Source 9.3 asks about two 60° angles plus a 4 cm side (one identical-copy shape), two right angles plus a 4 cm side (no triangle), and 60° and 90° plus an unspecified 4 cm side (multiple noncongruent shapes depending on which side is 4 cm).

Teacher-only human review is required for original drawings, measurements, choice of corresponding 4 cm segment, valid angle positioning and written/oral justification. A numeric answer or fixed RatioTable does not certify drawing quality, source exact-figure parity or academic acceptance. In Grade 7 students are not required to know the interior-angle-sum rule; the construction evidence can support explanations without that theorem.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number of possibilities
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given angles alone, the construction may have multiple different sizes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Drag, draw or trace at least two genuinely different sizes and compare which conditions stay true.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 75° angle alone does not select one triangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Impossible conditions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two distinct 90° interior angles cannot both occur in a nondegenerate triangle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Attempt a measured construction and show that the indicated rays do not meet in a third vertex.
KeyConcepts.Example: 90°, 90° and one side 4 cm: no triangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Side position matters
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two angle measures plus a side length fix a triangle shape only when the corresponding location of that side is fixed.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Label the endpoints of the 4 cm side and the adjacent angle vertices before comparing traces.
KeyConcepts.Example: 60°, 90° and some side 4 cm can describe more than one triangle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent drawing 1 — one angle
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw triangles having one interior angle of 75°. Do all such triangles have to be identical?
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct a 75° ray pair; choose two different distances along both rays and connect the resulting points.
Steps: Draw two rays meeting at 75° and mark one pair of endpoints at 3 cm and 4 cm from the vertex.
Draw a second triangle using points at 6 cm and 8 cm on the same rays.
Measure and explain that both have the prescribed 75° angle but their corresponding side lengths differ.
WorkedExamples.Answer: More than one noncongruent triangle; the angle alone does not fix scale.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher inspects two valid distinct-size constructions and angle measurement.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent drawing 2 — two angles
WorkedExamples.Question: Do interior angles of 75° and 45° alone force one triangle shape and size?
WorkedExamples.Method: Create one valid triangle, then make a scaled second drawing, keeping both measured angles unchanged.
Steps: Construct a triangle with a marked 75° angle at A and 45° angle at B, choosing an arbitrary positive AB.
Construct another using an AB twice as long, with the same two measured angles at their corresponding vertices.
Compare lengths by tracing or measurement: these drawings are not identical copies.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; there are multiple sizes unless a corresponding side length is also fixed.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks both angle measurements and distinct scale evidence; angle sum is not a prerequisite.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent drawing 3 — two 60 degree angles
WorkedExamples.Question: Two interior angles are 60° and one side is 4 cm. Can distinct-size triangles meet these conditions?
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct examples with a 4 cm side between two 60° rays and test candidate overlays.
Steps: Draw a 4 cm base and construct a 60° ray inward from each endpoint.
Complete the triangle where the rays meet and compare it with a peer's reflected or rotated copy.
Check that all three sides are 4 cm; reflection changes orientation but not the triangle's measurements.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One triangle shape up to rigid motion: an equilateral triangle with 4 cm sides.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews measured 4 cm sides and angle rays, and confirms the student's claim is about congruence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct and justify — zero, one or multiple triangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Using original drawings, compare: (A) two 60° angles and one 4 cm side; (B) two 90° angles and one 4 cm side; (C) 60° and 90° angles and an unspecified 4 cm side. How many noncongruent triangles are possible in each case?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw carefully using protractor and ruler. For case C, attach 4 cm to two different corresponding side positions and compare lengths.
Steps: For A, construct a 4 cm equilateral triangle; show all correctly drawn copies overlap after rotation/reflection.
For B, put two 90° rays at the ends of a baseline and explain why the rays cannot meet to make a third vertex.
For C, draw a right triangle with 4 cm between the 60° and 90° vertices, then a second with 4 cm between the 90° and 30° vertices; both meet the two given angles but their corresponding sides differ.
Explain how choosing which side is 4 cm changes the result, then submit both drawings and measured values for teacher review.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A: one shape; B: no triangle; C: multiple shapes when the measured side is not positioned.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher grades the original geometry, labeled side positions, scale, explanation and actual measurements. Do not auto-award construction credit based on answer A/B/C.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming two given angles force a unique size without a specified side.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The rays can be extended to construct different size triangles while keeping the measured angles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Make two scaled original constructions and compare corresponding side lengths.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Declaring two 90° interior angles a valid triangle or ignoring which corresponding side is 4 cm.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two right-angle rays on a common base cannot meet in a nondegenerate third vertex, while an unlocated side-length label is ambiguous.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check actual ray intersections and attach each given length to its correct labeled side before comparing models.

SummaryPoints: Draw with a ruler, protractor or dynamic geometry tool: one given angle or two given angles alone can allow different sizes.
Two 60° angles and a 4 cm side produce one equilateral triangle shape; two 90° angles cannot produce a triangle.
Two different angle measures and one side length may produce multiple different shapes if the corresponding side is unspecified; construction and teacher explanation matter.

Lessons.Title: Drawing Triangles (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks Grade 7 source-aligned goal: continue drawing triangles using two side lengths and an angle, or using three angle measures, and use original ruler/compass/protractor constructions to tell whether the data allow zero, one or multiple noncongruent triangles. Based on OUR/IM 2017–2019 Grade 7 lesson 7.7.10; student https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/7/10/index.html and teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/7/10/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 attribution; no publisher images copied).

V13 L10 source-specific repair: Construct a 40° angle, mark 5 cm along each ray and use a compass to compare the third side with 5 cm (it is shorter). Construct an independent right/obtuse triangle using the given 6-cm sides and a measured 100° INCLUDED angle, and compare traces. For a 45° angle with an 8-cm adjacent side and 6-cm opposite side, two distinct triangles can be constructed: the unspecified third side changes while the provided measurements stay fixed. The location of the given angle relative to two sides must be recorded; students should not be required to memorize theorem labels.

With only three angles 50°,60°,70°, drawings at different scales are possible, but the conditions 50°,60°,100° do not produce a triangle. Grade 7 students may justify using drawn rays, physical constructions and measurement without formal angle-sum or trigonometric formulas. Teacher evaluation is needed for actual drawings, angle labels, student evidence, reasoning, and rejection of malformed or degenerate sketches. A numeric answer or static table is not an automatic grade.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two sides and one measured angle
KeyConcepts.Definition: The locations of the two side lengths relative to the measured angle affect which and how many triangles can be built.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Draw the angle and mark the given lengths with a ruler or compass; test every viable endpoint intersection.
KeyConcepts.Example: A fixed nonincluded 45° angle and sides 8 cm and 6 cm can give two distinct triangles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Three given angles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three feasible angles alone can permit different-sized triangles, while incompatible angles cannot close.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Construct the angles, vary length and check that all three meet at proper noncollinear vertices.
KeyConcepts.Example: 50°,60°,70° permit scaled sizes; 50°,60°,100° do not form a triangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Check construction quality
KeyConcepts.Definition: A valid triangle must close with accurately labeled sides and angles.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use measured diagrams and compare with peers; count congruent copies as one shape regardless of orientation.
KeyConcepts.Example: For two sides 5 cm with 40° included, the third side is shorter than 5 cm.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent compass estimate — 40 degrees and two 5-cm sides
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw a 40° angle and mark 5 cm along each ray. Will the segment joining the endpoints be longer or shorter than 5 cm?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw and measure with ruler and compass; make an independent geometric comparison rather than requiring trigonometry.
Steps: Construct a measured 40° angle and mark each ray endpoint exactly 5 cm from the vertex.
Join the two endpoints. Compare the resulting third side with a 5-cm compass opening.
It is shorter than 5 cm (approximately 3.42 cm when accurately drawn).
WorkedExamples.Answer: The third side is shorter than 5 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks real compass/angle evidence. The approximate decimal is an independent oracle, not a required Grade 7 calculation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent drawing — two 6-cm sides with included 100 degrees
WorkedExamples.Question: Two 6-cm sides meet at a measured 100° included angle. Is there more than one triangle shape satisfying the same attachment and measurements?
WorkedExamples.Method: Mark 6 cm along both rays from a 100° vertex, then connect and overlay independently constructed triangles.
Steps: Draw two rays making a 100° angle and locate points 6 cm from their shared vertex.
Connect the two points, then try a second independent drawing using exactly the same three attached measurements.
Compare and overlay: the same two 6-cm sides and included angle determine one shape, up to rotation or reflection.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One triangle shape up to congruence.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews a genuine construction, included-angle position, units and peer overlay; no theorem name required.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent drawing — three angle measures
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare angle sets 50°,60°,70° and 50°,60°,100°. Which can form a triangle, and does a valid set fix its size?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw measured rays to see whether the triangle closes; compare different positive scales.
Steps: For 50°,60°,70°, draw one triangle and then a uniformly larger one with the same angles.
Use ruler and protractor or geometric explanation to compare their corresponding sides.
Try 50°,60°,100° with three interior angles; the three directions cannot close into a nondegenerate triangle.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher examines original angle constructions. A formal angle-sum theorem is optional at this grade level.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct and justify — nonincluded angle may give two triangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Fix a measured 45° angle at A, AB=8 cm, and BC=6 cm. Use a compass centered at B to find all possible points C on the 45° ray from A. How many different triangle shapes are there?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw original 45° ray, 8-cm side AB and a 6-cm arc from B; count distinct nondegenerate ray-circle intersections.
Steps: Draw AB=8 cm and a 45° ray from A above it.
Using radius 6 cm at B, mark each intersection of the circle with the ray; two distinct positive intersections exist.
Connect B to each candidate C, measure and record two different AC lengths (approximately 3.66 and 7.66 cm).
Show both satisfy AB=8 cm, BC=6 cm and angle A=45°, but their corresponding third sides differ, so the triangles are not congruent.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Two noncongruent valid triangles for this specified nonincluded-angle arrangement.
WorkedExamples.Check: Human teacher checks both actual triangle constructions, exact given labels and written explanation; do not score the count alone as full credit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming two side lengths and an angle always determine one triangle.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: When the given angle is not between the sides, an arc may cross the ray twice, once or not at all.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a compass at the stated center, test all ray-circle intersections and measure their corresponding sides.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating three angle measures as fixed triangle size, or believing nonclosing rays form a triangle.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Compatible angles allow scaling; incompatible angles cannot form a proper three-vertex polygon.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Construct rays with a geometry toolkit; verify nondegenerate closure and different scales before counting shapes.

SummaryPoints: Drawing 40° between two 5-cm sides gives a connecting third side shorter than 5 cm; verify with a compass.
Two side lengths and a given angle can produce one or multiple shapes depending on how the angle is attached.
Three compatible angles alone allow different scales; some angle triples cannot close into a triangle. Submit original drawings for human review.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct and justify — Building Prisms
WorkedExamples.Question: A right triangular prism has a 3–4–5 cm right-triangle base and prism length 8 cm. Draw a net, compute volume and exterior area, and state a possible horizontal cross-section.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw an independent accurate geometry model, measure or construct required angles/sides/cross-sections, calculate and justify, and submit for teacher review.
Steps: The two matching triangular bases each have area (3×4)/2=6 cm².
Wrap three lateral rectangles 3×8,4×8,5×8 cm around the triangle; lateral area=96 cm².
Total surface area=2×6+96=108 cm²; volume=6×8=48 cm³.
Draw both triangles and all three correctly connected rectangular panels; slice parallel to the triangular bases gives a congruent triangle.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Volume 48 cm³, surface 108 cm²; parallel cross-section a 3–4–5 triangle.
